You know, economics is in many ways voodoo. People are irrational, and some of the brightest minds in economics have come up with ideas that in hindsight were completely wrong. For instance I have enormous respect for Milton Friedman, yet I think at this point in time we can say that supply side economics has simply not worked. The rich have gotten incredibly wealthy, but the jobs and investments that this was supposed to spurn just simply never really materialized - and now the working class is actually starting to become poorer. It was an intelligent and logically fashioned idea, but economics is not such a tame beast as to obey our logic inclinings.

So I think the best response here is to simply look at what happens in real life. And fortunately we have a great example, even in the states! Alaska has as close as we've come to a large scale basic income in the states. In the late 60s in Alaska massive amounts of oil were discovered. The government there then leased these oil fields out to private enterprise and saw a huge windfall of income. Predictably they completely squandered it. The residents of the state were not particularly happy with this and this led to the creation of the Alaska Permanent Fund. This is a state owned but privately managed enterprise that is given a certain amount of money each year to invest that includes a fraction of the revenue from the oil sales. The company then invests this money and the returns are split equally across every man, woman, and child in the Alaska each year. The payouts have peaked at $3,200 and average around $1,500. The average household in Alaska has 2.79 people meaning each household has gotten up to $9000 in a year and averages about $4,200 per year. Not basic income scale, but still a very real amount of money that ought at least start to show us an inclining of inflation.

Now this makes all of that even more interesting. That's the consumer price index, a typical measurement of inflation, for Alaska contrasted against the USA. In spite of the fact that each household in Alaska is simply given thousands of dollars each and every year, their inflation has actually increased more slowly than the US as a whole. Goods are still pricey in Alaska due to large transport/shipping costs, but those costs have increased proportionally slower than the US as a whole. If the market was simply increasing costs because people could afford to pay proportionally more, this is not what we'd expect to see.
